current_answer: Choose cache policy in this order: decide whether the response is private or safely shared; set browser max-age and, separately, shared-cache s-maxage when needed; add ETag or Last-Modified for cheap validation; then test every request input that can change the body. Under HTTP, s-maxage controls shared freshness before max-age and Expires, while a private cache does not use s-maxage as its lifetime. For a named CloudFront standard distribution, inspect the matching behavior and effective MinTTL/DefaultTTL/MaxTTL: explicit origin freshness is bounded by that policy, and a positive MinTTL can make the edge cache despite origin no-cache, no-store, or private. AWS identifies s-maxage as an origin TTL input, but its detailed worked table does not spell out the standalone s-maxage-only shape; treat the bounded edge result as an expected, documentation-grounded reading rather than an observation. A response-headers policy changes the viewer response and does not prove the edge TTL. Tie invalidation query paths to the effective cache key, name rewrites precisely, and poll GetInvalidation until Completed; that is CloudFront-operation evidence, not a purge of browsers or other downstream hops. For stale validation, If-None-Match wins whenever it is present: a matching ETag can produce 304, while a nonmatching ETag does not fall back to the date. This CloudFront audit remains documentation-only with no live distribution measurement or invalidation.

catalogue_card.question: How can web developers choose correct HTTP cache headers and diagnose stale content without accidentally caching private responses?
catalogue_card.text: Separate storage audience, freshness, validation, and variant matching. Use the cache-key/privacy worksheet before sharing responses, and treat hits, Age, and Cache-Status as evidence from a named hop—not as proof of safety. For an old display, separate lifecycle and worker evidence from named intermediary and origin observations before calling it a cache hit.

summary: Fresh reuse may make no network request; stale reuse usually leads to validation.
304 keeps the stored representation while 200 replaces it; If-None-Match takes precedence over If-Modified-Since.
The minimum key model is method plus target URI; query components normally make distinct targets, but extra normalization/keying is deployment-specific.
Vary constrains matching of nominated request fields, including missing versus present values; Vary: * fails ordinary matching without revalidation.
Cookie is not automatically part of the HTTP minimum key, and Set-Cookie alone is not a cache barrier; personalized bodies should start private.
Authorization needs explicit shared-reuse permission (public, s-maxage, or must-revalidate), but permission is not proof that a user-specific representation is safe to share.
A redacted A/B marker plus same-hop Cache-Control, Vary, Set-Cookie, Age, Cache-Status, and Via evidence is a practical pre-deploy check.
A pageshow persisted reactivation with no request supports history/bfcache, while a worker log can identify a Cache API hit or synthesized response in that client.
A named Cache-Status hit is scoped evidence from that intermediary; Age corroborates when present, Via identifies forwarding, and missing fields are unknown.
For a named CloudFront behavior, effective MinTTL/DefaultTTL/MaxTTL settings bound the nominal edge result; s-maxage controls shared freshness while browser max-age remains separate.

AWS explicitly documents that a positive CloudFront minimum can override origin no-cache, no-store, or private; keep MinTTL at zero for sensitive paths and review the effective behavior rather than only viewer headers.
The standalone s-maxage-only CloudFront shape has a narrow AWS documentation gap: RFC 9111 resolves the shared-cache semantics, but no live product result is claimed.
A response-headers policy changes the viewer response only; its Cache-Control value is not evidence of edge TTL or edge non-storage.
Invalidate according to the behavior’s effective cache key and rewrite scope; record the path list and ID and poll GetInvalidation to Completed.
Use a new fingerprinted URL for frequently changing public assets; use a narrow path invalidation for stable HTML or urgent edge refresh, and name the downstream limits.
The CloudFront audit and all earlier follow-ups remain documentation-only or expected/model outputs; no live distribution, invalidation, or downstream purge was observed.
uncertainty: The cache-key worksheet and model outcomes are standards-based expectations and synthetic model output; no live curl/socket capture was available for this run.
Standards do not force every cache to store or reuse a response; browser, service-worker, CDN, reverse-proxy, framework, partitioning, and vendor behavior varies.
The minimum key does not prescribe query normalization or other extra key material; Vary cannot cover unlisted application state.
Age and Cache-Status are useful only when exposed by the responding path; their absence is not proof that no cache exists or that an origin was contacted.
Authorization permission, Vary: Cookie, a 200/304, or a model hit is not a confidentiality guarantee and cannot establish absence of leakage.
Service-worker/Cache API keys are separate from HTTP cache keys; history/bfcache can show old DOM without a new request; a direct client is not a browser topology.
One A/B marker test cannot establish that all alternate keys, redirects, concurrent races, POPs, partitions, or uninstrumented layers are safe.
CloudFront TTL, response-header, Server-Timing, invalidation, quota, and versioning claims are product-specific documentation claims for a named configuration, not universal HTTP/CDN behavior.
The exact CloudFront behavior, cache policy, effective m/d/M values, viewer header transformation, POP, hit/miss, object residency, and downstream copies were not observed.

No live CloudFront measurement or invalidation was performed: no AWS account/distribution, authorized endpoint, origin counter, client capture, invalidation ID/status, versioned rollout, or cost/quota usage was available.

The standalone s-maxage-only CloudFront product behavior and its viewer-header interaction remain unobserved; AWS’s detailed table shows the paired max-age+s-maxage row, while RFC 9111 resolves only the shared-cache semantics.
A response-headers policy can add or override a viewer Cache-Control header without changing how CloudFront caches the object; viewer headers cannot prove edge storage or non-storage.
Invalidation query coverage depends on the effective cache key, not merely origin-request forwarding; rewrite-stage and directory slash forms require deployment-specific inspection.

CloudFront invalidation Completed is evidence about the named CloudFront operation only; it does not prove that browsers, history/bfcache, service workers, corporate proxies, other CDNs, or other hops discarded an old URL.
No live layer attribution was obtained: curl and browsers were absent, no authorized endpoint was supplied, and a Node loopback listener failed with EPERM.

A positive layer observation is scoped to one client, URL/key, request, time, and topology; it does not prove absence of other POPs, partitions, hidden hops, request collapsing, or cross-user leakage.
